title: The science of men
hook: scholars wrote lives of the narrators, to test each one

segments.voice: Yesterday, mutawatir, and your line: so many said it. When you felt certain of something, was it one voice or many? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A story is told about the hadith scholar Ali ibn al-Madini. Someone asked him about a narrator, and the narrator was his own father. He hesitated, and said: ask someone else. They pressed him. And he answered, as the story goes: this is the religion. My father is weak. Whatever the details, the story shows what a whole field of study asked of people. A son, asked a question, chose accuracy over family pride. Behind that answer was a library of judgments about people. Today, the science of men.
screen: `ASKED ABOUT HIS OWN FATHER.` → `THIS IS THE RELIGION.` → `A LIBRARY ABOUT PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Rijal means men, and in hadith study it names the narrators themselves, the people in the chains. Despite the word, the books include women who narrated too. Second, why it began. In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the early scholar Ibn Sirin is quoted saying, in effect: people didn't use to ask about chains. Then came the time of turmoil, and they said: name your men for us. And Ibn Sirin again: this knowledge is religion, so look at whom you take your religion from. Third, what the books record. Scholars wrote entry after entry, narrator by narrator. Where he lived. Whom he heard from, and who heard from him. Whether he traveled. Was he truthful? Was his memory precise, or did it slip, or did it fade late in life? Did he write his reports down, and keep the pages safe? The field has a blunt name: al-jarh wa al-ta'dil, wounding and vouching. Each narrator could be wounded by a scholar's criticism, or vouched for. Fourth, a hard question the scholars faced openly. Isn't talking about a man's flaws a kind of backbiting? Imam Muslim answers in that same introduction: exposing a narrator's weakness, to protect what's said in the Prophet's name, isn't forbidden backbiting. It's a duty. And, as the story goes, some applied it even to their own fathers. Out of this came books of narrators that students of hadith still open. When a scholar grades a report, this is the shelf behind the grade.
screen: `RIJAL: THE PEOPLE IN THE CHAINS.` · `NAME YOUR MEN FOR US.` · `WOUNDING AND VOUCHING.` · `NOT BACKBITING, A DUTY.`

segments.voice: The practice: check a source's reputation. Settle, and breathe. Pick one voice you trust for information. A news outlet, a teacher, a channel, a friend who always knows things. Now ask the rijal questions about them, quietly. Where did they get what they tell me? Have they been wrong before, and did they say so? Is their memory careful, or do details drift? Do they have a reason to shade the story? You're not putting them on trial. You're writing a short entry in your own book of narrators. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in judging. The bell holds the time.
Rijal. Literally men: the narrators in the chains, and the science of studying who each one was and whether he can be trusted. Today's word.
Your line: who was he? Today, before you share something, look up one thing about who first said it. Tomorrow: the traveling scholars. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Hadith scholars consult biographical dictionaries of narrators, the books of rijal, to check each name in a chain for honesty, memory and whom they met, a field called al-jarh wa al-ta'dil.
